paragraphs: Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam, Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu, is a Hindu temple dedicated to Ranganatha, the reclining form of the god Vishnu. Situated on an island formed by the Kaveri and Kollidam rivers, it is generally regarded as the largest functioning Hindu temple in the world, its walled complex covering roughly 63 hectares (156 acres).

The temple is the first and foremost of the 108 Divya Desams — the Vishnu temples glorified in the Naalayira Divya Prabandham, the early-medieval Tamil canon of the Alvar saints. It is a principal centre of the Sri Vaishnava tradition and was the seat of the philosopher Ramanuja in the 11th–12th centuries.

Built and expanded over more than a millennium under the Chola, Pandya, Hoysala, Vijayanagara and Nayak dynasties, the complex contains seven concentric prakaras (enclosures), 21 gopurams (gateway towers), and numerous mandapams (pillared halls). Its 13-tiered Rajagopuram, completed in 1987, rises about 72 metres, making it one of the tallest temple towers in Asia.

According to the temple's Sthalapurana, the Ranga Vimana — the shrine housing Ranganatha — was originally worshipped by the solar dynasty and given by Rama to Vibhishana; while resting on the Kaveri island during his journey to Lanka, the deity chose to remain facing south toward Lanka, and the shrine was established at Srirangam.

Historically, Srirangam is mentioned in Sangam-era literature, and the temple's fame grew through the hymns of the Alvar saints (6th–9th centuries CE), who dedicated more verses to Ranganatha of Srirangam than to any other deity. Epigraphic records document continuous endowments from the Chola and Pandya periods onwards.

The temple was sacked during the invasions of the Delhi Sultanate in 1311 (Malik Kafur) and again in 1323. The presiding image was carried away and the temple's traditions disrupted; the deity was restored to Srirangam in 1371 under early Vijayanagara patronage. The following three centuries — under the Vijayanagara empire and the Nayaks of Madurai — saw the greatest expansion of the complex: outer prakaras, gopurams, and grand mandapams.
In 2017 the temple received the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award of Merit for cultural heritage conservation, recognising the restoration of the complex using traditional methods and materials.

The complex is a textbook of Dravidian temple architecture at urban scale: seven rectangular prakaras (concentric walled enclosures) wrap the sanctum, the outermost measuring over 3 kilometres in perimeter. The three outer enclosures contain streets, houses and shops — the living town of Srirangam — while the four inner enclosures are strictly religious space.

The complex has 21 gopurams. The southern Rajagopuram, left unfinished for centuries as a massive base, was completed by the 44th Jeer of the Ahobila Matha in 1987; at about 72 metres (236 ft) over 13 tiers, it dominates the skyline of Tiruchirappalli.

Notable structures include the Hall of 1000 Pillars (actually 953 pillars of granite, a Vijayanagara-period composition), the Sesharayar Mandapam with its dramatic rearing-horse monolith pillars, the gold-plated Ranga Vimana over the sanctum, and shrines to Ranganayaki Thayar, Chakrathazhwar, and the Vaishnava acharyas, including the shrine where the preserved form of Ramanuja is venerated.

Srirangam is the foremost of the 108 Divya Desams and one of the most important pilgrimage centres of Sri Vaishnavism. It is celebrated as 'Bhooloka Vaikuntam' — Vaikuntha (Vishnu's celestial abode) on earth — and as the first of the Pancharanga Kshetrams, the five Ranganatha temples along the Kaveri.

The Alvar saints composed 247 pasurams (hymns) on Ranganatha of Srirangam in the Naalayira Divya Prabandham. The temple is intimately associated with Andal, who according to tradition merged with the deity here, and with Thiruppan Alvar. Ramanuja systematised the temple's administration and worship in the 11th–12th centuries; the Pancharatra agama governs its rituals to this day.

Devotees hold that darshan of Ranganatha at Srirangam, especially through the Paramapada Vasal (Gate of Vaikuntha) on Vaikunta Ekadasi, confers liberation (moksha). The temple is thus a principal destination for Vaishnava pilgrimage in South India and among diaspora communities worldwide.

The temple is administered by the Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department of the Government of Tamil Nadu, through an Executive Officer and a Board of Trustees. Daily worship follows the Pancharatra agama, conducted by hereditary priest families.

The temple operates guest houses, annadanam (free food) programmes, an elephant, a museum, and a heritage conservation cell. Official communication, seva bookings and e-donation facilities are provided through the HR&CE portal.

The temple accepts donations for annadanam, renovation (thiruppani), festival sponsorship, and general endowment through the official HR&CE channels. Sevas such as archana, abhishekam and vahana processions may be booked at the temple counters or online.
Through this directory, devotees may additionally sponsor an Akhand Deepam — a continuously burning lamp — in their name or their family's name (see the Light a Lamp section below).

steps.title: Before You Enter
points: Bathe and wear clean traditional clothing; many pilgrims bathe in the Kaveri before darshan.
Dress code: men — dhoti/pyjama or trousers with upper cloth or shirt; women — saree, half-saree or salwar kameez. Shorts, sleeveless tops and lungis are not permitted.
Carry offerings if you wish: tulsi garland, flowers, coconut, camphor and incense are customary for Vishnu.
Footwear must be deposited at the stands outside the outer prakara; mobile phones should be silenced.

steps.title: At the Entrance (Rajagopuram)
points: Enter through the southern Rajagopuram gateway, stepping in with the right foot first, per tradition.
Offer respects at the Dwajasthambam (golden flag post) in the inner court with folded hands.
Pradakshina (circumambulation) is always clockwise; pilgrims traditionally walk the inner prakaras.
On festival days, follow the queue signage — the temple operates separate free and paid darshan queues.

steps.title: Inside the Temple Premises
points: Customary order: Chakrathazhwar and Garuda sannidhi, then Ranganayaki Thayar shrine, before proceeding to the main sanctum — at Divya Desams the Thayar is traditionally worshipped first.
Visit the Ramanuja shrine in the fourth prakara, where the acharya's preserved form is venerated.
Stand with palms joined (anjali mudra) at each shrine; recite the deity's names or pasurams softly.
Do not touch the deities, the dhwajasthambam, or festival vahanas.

steps.title: Main Deity Darshan (Ranganatha)
points: Approach the Garbhagriha through the Gayatri Mandapam; the reclining Ranganatha is viewed feet-first — let your gaze rest at the lotus feet before moving to the face.
Chant 'Om Namo Narayanaya' or the Ranganatha Gadyam as you stand before the sanctum.
Receive theertham (holy water) in a cupped right hand over the left, sip, and touch the hand to your eyes; receive prasadam with both hands cupped.
Do not linger at the sanctum doorway during heavy queues; a calm, brief darshan is traditional.

steps.title: Sevas & Abhishekam
points: Archana (name-and-nakshatra puja) may be booked at the counters in the inner prakara.
Abhishekam and Thirumanjanam sponsorships are available on published days; book in advance at the Devasthanam office or online via the HR&CE portal.
Viswaroopa Seva (early-morning first darshan, 06:00) and Ekanta Seva (night) are especially valued; arrive 30 minutes early.
Prasadam — the temple's famed puliyodarai (tamarind rice) and sweet pongal — is available at the official counters.

steps.title: What Not to Do & Before Leaving
points: Photography is prohibited inside the inner prakaras and sanctum; leather items, tobacco, alcohol and non-vegetarian food must not be brought into the complex.
Non-Hindus may visit the outer prakaras but are not admitted into the sanctum, per temple custom.
Complete a final pradakshina and offer a lamp at the lamp stands if you wish.
When leaving the sanctum, avoid turning your back to the deity immediately — step aside first; sit for a few minutes in the mandapam before exiting the temple.

entryGuidelines: Traditional dress required; western formal wear is tolerated in outer prakaras but not for special sevas.
Free darshan queue operates all day; paid quick-darshan tickets are available at the counters.
Elderly and differently-abled devotees may use the wheelchair assistance and separate queue at the main gate.

specialRituals.description: Personalised puja with the devotee's name, gotra and nakshatra recited by the priest.
Ceremonial bath of the utsava deity with milk, curd, honey and sandal on published days.
Sponsor a procession of the deity on one of the temple's vahanas (mounts) during festivals.
Sponsor free meals served daily to devotees.

restrictions: No photography or videography beyond the outer prakaras.
No leather goods, footwear, tobacco, alcohol or non-vegetarian food inside the complex.
Sanctum entry restricted to Hindus, per temple custom.
Mobile phones must be silent; calls are not permitted in the inner prakaras.
spiritualOutcomes: Moksha (liberation) — darshan through the Paramapada Vasal on Vaikunta Ekadasi is believed to confer liberation.
Removal of obstacles and ancestral blessings — associated with worship of Ranganatha with tulsi.
Marital harmony and family welfare — attributed to worship of Ranganayaki Thayar.

festivals.name: Vaikunta Ekadasi (Pagal Pathu & Ra Pathu)
festivals.description: The temple's greatest festival. The Paramapada Vasal (Gate of Vaikuntha) is opened, and Ranganatha in pearl armour passes through it; hundreds of thousands attend. The Araiyar Sevai recital of the Divya Prabandham is performed.

festivals.name: Chithirai Brahmotsavam (Viruppan Thirunal)
festivals.description: Grand annual festival with daily vahana processions and the car (ther) festival through the Chithirai streets.

festivals.name: Jyeshtabhishekam
festivals.description: Annual ceremonial cleansing and re-anointment of the utsava deity.

festivals.name: Andal Adi Pooram
festivals.description: Celebrates Andal, the poet-saint bride of Ranganatha.

festivals.name: Panguni Uthiram
festivals.description: Divine wedding festival; the only day Ranganatha and Ranganayaki grant joint darshan (serthi seva).

visitingInfo.bestTime: November to March; Margazhi (Dec–Jan) for Vaikunta Ekadasi, though crowds are largest then.
visitingInfo.dressCode: Traditional attire; shoulders and knees covered. Dhoti/saree recommended for sevas.

howToReach.rail: Srirangam railway station (1 km) on the Chennai–Tiruchirappalli line; Tiruchirappalli Junction 9 km.
howToReach.road: City buses and autos from Tiruchirappalli; NH-38/Chennai–Trichy highways.

visitingInfo.entryFee: Free darshan; paid quick-darshan tickets available. Viewpoint ticket separate.
nearbyAttractions: Rockfort Ucchi Pillayar Temple, Trichy (8 km)

reviews.author: Devotee from Chennai
reviews.text: Attended Vaikunta Ekadasi — passing through the Paramapada Vasal is an experience beyond words. Plan for long queues.

reviews.author: Pilgrim from Singapore
reviews.text: The scale of the seven prakaras is humbling. The Viswaroopa Seva at dawn is serene; the puliyodarai prasadam is a must.

reviews.author: Visitor from Bengaluru
reviews.text: Beautifully maintained. The 1000-pillar hall and the museum deserve an unhurried hour each.
